entities.name: Ankhefensekhmet
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ankhefensekhmet (ˁnḫ=f n sḫm.t), whose name translates as 'He lives for Sekhmet,' held the prestigious office of High Priest of Ptah in Memphis during a complex and transitional period of ancient Egyptian history, specifically the 21st Dynasty. While precise dates for his tenure remain elusive, he most likely served during the reign of Psusennes II (c. 967–943 BCE) and potentially continued into the early years of Shoshenq I (c. 943–922 BCE), marking his presence at the cusp of the Third Intermediate Period and the advent of the Libyan (22nd) Dynasty. His significance lies in his role as a key religious and administrative figure in Memphis, a traditional capital and spiritual heartland, at a time when royal power was increasingly fragmented and regional authorities, particularly high priests, wielded substantial influence.

As High Priest of Ptah, Ankhefensekhmet would have been responsible for the vast temple estates dedicated to the Memphite god, overseeing their economic resources, personnel, and elaborate rituals that were central to Egyptian cosmic order. His duties included performing daily rites, managing the temple’s considerable wealth, and maintaining the cult of Ptah, Sekhmet, and Nefertem. In an era where the pharaoh's direct control diminished, the High Priests of Ptah, alongside the High Priests of Amun in Thebes, became de facto regional rulers, often engaging in political maneuvering and dynastic alliances to secure their positions and influence royal succession, even if such direct involvement by Ankhefensekhmet is not explicitly documented.
